skill_gap: Digital asset discovery and inventory navigation
explanation: This capability is the ability to systematically search enterprise data inventories, metadata repositories, system catalogues, and reusable digital components before starting new development. In future work, staff must use standardized and increasingly AI-enabled discovery tools to assess what data, concepts, and processing assets already exist, determine suitability and reusability, and document why any new build or collection is necessary. It supports more efficient needs identification, concept alignment, and data availability assessment across GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts the organization toward digital-first, reusable, automated, and evidence-based decision making. Those change drivers influence GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 by requiring staff to scan existing data holdings, standardized concepts, and reusable tools before proposing new solutions, with documented justification, metadata-supported discovery, and stronger triage of cost, impact, sustainability, and automation fit. The current work emphasizes development and implementation, but not the mandatory pre-development discovery and inventory navigation now required.

explanation: This capability is the ability to assess whether a need should be met by reusing existing data, enhancing current systems, applying automation, or building something new, and to clearly document why the chosen option is the best operational fit. In practice, it adds a mandatory pre-development stage to identify needs and check data availability and suitability, using enterprise tools, metadata, and standardized review processes before any new development proceeds. It also supports future modular delivery by ensuring processing and analysis components are selected or built based on reusability, feasibility, auditability, and alignment with enterprise platforms.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires stronger evidence-based decision-making before launching new collection or development work. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 3.2, these change drivers point to a future state where staff must systematically scan existing data assets, administrative and alternative sources, and reusable digital components, then justify any net-new solution through documented cost, impact, reusability, automation, and strategic fit analysis. As a result, future work requirements are shifting from defaulting to bespoke development toward enterprise reuse, standardized governance, and auditable solution justification.

skill_gap: AI and automation applicability in statistical operations
explanation: This capability is the ability to identify where AI, rules-based automation, and enterprise digital workflow tools can replace or strengthen manual or custom-built statistical processing work before new development begins. In practice, it supports a mandatory pre-development assessment of existing data assets, reusable components, and approved automation options so that processing and analysis designs are modular, auditable, metadata-driven, and suitable for automated editing, imputation, and near real-time operations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the StatCan 2030 Future Slide for GSBPM 2.5, 1.5, and 5.4 requires staff to assess reusable enterprise assets first, design machine-actionable and standardized workflows, and oversee AI-enabled automated processing rather than defaulting to manual or custom development. It is also driven by the Mandate letters and Departmental Plan emphasis on modernization, efficiency, interoperability, and responsible use of digital and data capabilities, which together make early evaluation of AI and automation applicability a required step in determining how future statistical work will be designed and delivered.

skill_gap: Federated data sourcing and enterprise data reuse
explanation: This capability is the ability to identify, assess, and reuse internal, administrative, alternative, and external data sources across the enterprise before proposing new collection. It supports more rigorous needs identification, automated data availability and suitability checks, and modular reuse of collection or extraction approaches by using metadata, digital workflows, and evidence-based decision rules. In practice, staff must understand how federated data ecosystems and enterprise assets can meet emerging requirements quickly, consistently, and with less reliance on bespoke surveys.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide expects staff to default to enterprise reuse, federated sourcing, automation, and digitally enabled triage before initiating new collection. It is also reinforced by Mandate letter drivers for more efficient, responsive, and evidence-based government services, which increase the need to systematically assess internal and external data options, document why new surveys are necessary, and support automated, auditable decisions in activities such as identifying needs, checking data availability, and reusing or building collection instruments.

explanation: Digital operating model assessment is the capability to determine whether a new requirement should be met by replacing a system, redesigning a process, automating tasks, or integrating with existing enterprise workflows and data assets. It supports more rigorous decision-making in needs identification, workflow design, and evaluation by requiring staff to assess reuse, interoperability, automation fit, and evidence from existing systems before proposing new or bespoke solutions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a more digital, integrated, and sustainable operating environment where reuse, automation, and enterprise-wide coordination must be considered before new collection or system investment is approved. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 2.6, and 8.2 by requiring staff to triage needs against existing assets, design modular and interoperable workflows, and use continuous evaluation evidence to justify whether replacement, redesign, or automation is the appropriate response.

skill_gap: Structured intake and requirements triage facilitation
explanation: This capability is the ability to lead stakeholders through a consistent intake and needs-identification process that clarifies the problem, reviews existing data and systems, assesses reuse options, and applies feasibility criteria before new work is approved. It supports more formal, evidence-based consultation by requiring staff to use asset scans, metadata-enabled discovery, cost-benefit and impact analysis, and enterprise constraints to determine whether existing sources can meet the need before proposing new collections or bespoke solutions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more integrated, efficient, and digitally enabled decision-making, with stronger expectations to reuse existing data, reduce duplication, and apply automation and enterprise standards early in the process. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to facilitate standardized triage, challenge assumptions that new requests need new systems or surveys, and document evidence-based decisions using metadata, feasibility screening, and strategic prioritization before project planning proceeds.

explanation: Decision-support communication is the ability to translate asset scans, feasibility assessments, reuse options, risks, and cost-benefit evidence into clear advice that helps users and managers make informed intake and governance decisions. In future needs identification, consultation, and user support work, this means guiding stakeholders through standardized, evidence-based discussions using metadata platforms, enterprise criteria, and documented trade-offs rather than relying on assumptions or procedural habits.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 7.5 requires staff to challenge default assumptions about new surveys, synthesize evidence from digital discovery and metadata tools, and communicate clear recommendations at formal decision points. This is directly influenced by the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize modernization, reuse of existing data assets, digital service delivery, transparency, and stronger enterprise prioritization—raising the need for officers to communicate evidence-based options, constraints, and impacts clearly to support governance and planning.

explanation: Enterprise metadata and interoperability standards are the capability to apply common metadata practices, FAIR principles, and interoperability rules so data, concepts, and assets can be discovered, reused, integrated, and exchanged across programs and systems. In practice, this means staff can work with AI-enabled discovery tools, metadata repositories, and standardized integration architectures to validate concepts, assess data suitability, and support automated, auditable data integration with minimal manual rework.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 5.1 depends on standardized metadata, enterprise reuse, and interoperable digital architectures, while the current role framing does not yet reflect that broader enterprise contribution. The need is directly driven by Mandate letters emphasizing digital government and service integration, the Departmental Plan’s focus on modernized data and digital operations, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide direction toward AI-enabled, FAIR, reusable, and interoperable statistical production, which together increase expectations for staff to represent metadata and interoperability requirements in cross-departmental governance and design decisions.

skill_gap: Pre-project governance and gated delivery leadership
explanation: This capability is the ability to lead work before implementation begins by guiding structured initiation, feasibility assessment, evidence gathering, and formal approval through defined governance gates. It requires leaders to build clear business rationale, align action plans with accountable decision points, and ensure proposed work is feasible, traceable, auditable, and ready to support modular, automated, and governed delivery environments.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively push work toward faster, more transparent, and digitally governed decision-making, which moves leadership upstream from execution into pre-project assessment and approval. The future work described in GSBPM 8.3, 7.3, and 2.6 requires leaders to justify investments through standardized evidence, governance checkpoints, auditability, interoperability, and readiness for automated, platform-based operations, making pre-project governance and gated delivery leadership a critical future requirement.

explanation: Multi-criteria feasibility assessment is the capability to evaluate a proposed data or statistical response across operational, technical, data, automation, cost, risk, and sustainability dimensions at the same time, rather than from a single subject-matter perspective. In practice, this means staff must assess existing data availability and suitability, automation and AI compatibility, enterprise resource implications, and whether new collection is justified before advancing needs identification, source selection, or processing design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5 requires broader, evidence-based decisions that integrate data discovery, reuse, automation readiness, legal/privacy context, and modular system design before recommending action. This direction is driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize modernization, responsible use of administrative and alternative data, automation/AI adoption, efficiency, and sustainable enterprise-wide decision-making, thereby expanding future work requirements beyond the current decision frame.

explanation: This capability is the ability to diagnose the root cause of a business or data problem and map it to the most appropriate intervention, such as reusing existing data assets, improving metadata, integrating systems, automating workflows, redesigning processes, or developing something new. In future work across identifying needs, identifying concepts, and reusing or building components, staff must assess options early, use enterprise inventories and AI-enabled discovery tools, and justify when new collection or bespoke system changes are truly required.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state direction in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide emphasizes reuse before new collection, enterprise integration, automation, standardization, and faster digitally enabled decision-making. Those change drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 3.2 by requiring staff to evaluate problems across data, metadata, process, and technology layers, rather than defaulting to technical fixes or new development recommendations.

explanation: Business case and justification writing is the capability to produce concise, decision-ready documentation that clearly explains why a proposed change is needed and why it is better than reusing existing assets, using alternative data sources, or adopting automated and digital options. In the future state, this requires officers to build evidence-based cases using cost-benefit, risk, and outcome analysis, while supporting faster governance decisions, transparent trade-offs, and action planning tied to ongoing evaluation and dashboard-based monitoring.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive expectations for modernization, automation, reuse of existing data assets, and faster, more transparent decision-making. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.6, 8.2, and 8.3 by requiring formal comparative justification, alignment with enterprise platforms and AI-enabled approaches, and action plans that are traceable, measurable, and continuously monitored rather than supported by discretionary or narrative-based rationale.

skill_gap: Digital product lifecycle and upstream delivery planning
explanation: This capability is the ability to plan digital work as one connected lifecycle, from intake and needs identification through discovery, feasibility, governance, implementation, and release. It includes aligning people, milestones, tools, and decision points early so that metadata review, enterprise scanning, business-case development, automation readiness, and governed dissemination can be built into delivery plans rather than added later. In practice, it supports a shift from ad hoc project starts and manual release activity toward structured upstream analysis, platform-based workflows, and monitored, auditable delivery.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, enterprise-wide, and automation-enabled ways of working, which increase the importance of planning work before formal project execution begins. The future-state requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 7.3, and 7.4 show that teams must resource digital scanning, metadata-assisted discovery, feasibility documentation, governed release workflows, and analytics-enabled dissemination from the outset. These change drivers therefore influence future work by shifting priorities and staffing toward earlier discovery, integrated governance, and lifecycle planning across both delivery and dissemination.

explanation: Cost-benefit-risk analysis is the capability to assess and compare reuse, automation, integration, and new development options by weighing their financial, operational, sustainability, and risk implications before implementation begins. In practice, this supports stronger decision-making in identifying needs, preparing business cases, and selecting or building processing components by ensuring choices are evidence-based, reusable, auditable, and aligned with enterprise platforms and automated workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires earlier and more formal trade-off analysis at the design stage, rather than focusing mainly on implementation costs. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.6, and 3.2, these change drivers increase expectations to justify reuse over new collection, assess automation and integration options, and support modular enterprise solutions with transparent cost, benefit, sustainability, and risk comparisons.

explanation: This capability is the ability to assess digital solutions not only for immediate fit, but also for long-term sustainability, including maintainability, reuse, integration potential, automation compatibility, and avoidance of duplicate or bespoke approaches. In activities such as identifying needs, consulting on options, and checking data availability, staff must compare existing assets and proposed solutions through structured cost-benefit-risk analysis so that decisions support efficient, reusable, and sustainable operations over time.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires feasibility assessments to explicitly consider sustainability, reuse, automation, and enterprise-wide efficiency before new collection or custom development proceeds. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5, these change drivers shift work toward formalized, evidence-based triage of needs and data options, making sustainability-informed digital solution assessment essential for budgeting, prioritization, and justification of future work.

explanation: Evidence-based requirements elicitation is the capability to identify and confirm stakeholder needs by testing requests against existing data assets, metadata, enterprise standards, feasibility criteria, and operational constraints before proposing new collection. In GSBPM 1.1 and 1.2, this means using digital discovery tools, structured challenge, and cost-benefit discussions to jointly validate needs; in 8.2, it is reinforced by evaluation evidence, dashboards, and past performance insights that inform whether requirements are realistic, reusable, and sustainable.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a more digital, efficient, and evidence-based model of service delivery in which new requests must be assessed against existing capabilities, automation potential, and enterprise priorities before new work is launched. These change drivers influence future work requirements by making intake, consultation, and evaluation more formalized, metadata-enabled, and analytically rigorous, requiring staff to move from simply gathering requirements to validating them through feasibility, reuse, impact, and sustainability criteria.

explanation: This capability is the ability to turn discovery work, metadata evidence, asset audits, and option analysis into clear executive-ready recommendations on whether to proceed, reuse existing assets, change a process, or invest in new development. It supports future work in needs identification, needs confirmation, and design by helping staff synthesize feasibility, cost-benefit, reusability, and strategic fit into concise decision briefings for approval and prioritization.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more rigorous, digitally enabled decision-making before new collection or development is approved. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 2.5, these change drivers require staff to use metadata platforms, enterprise asset discovery, automation-compatible design, and explicit cost-impact-reuse assessments, which increases the need to synthesize technical findings into executive briefings that guide prioritization and justify reuse or process change over bespoke solutions.

explanation: Metadata standards and data cataloguing capability enables staff to consistently describe, locate, assess, and reuse data assets across the enterprise before creating new collections or systems. In future work across identifying needs, identifying concepts, and checking data availability and suitability, staff must use standardized metadata, inventories, and AI-enabled discovery tools to support rapid, evidence-based decisions, federated access, and FAIR data practices.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a future operating model that prioritizes enterprise data reuse, digital integration, automation, and reduced reliance on new survey collection. Those change drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 by requiring machine-actionable metadata, standardized cataloguing, and discovery mechanisms so staff can systematically identify existing assets, align to reusable concepts, and justify new collection only when no suitable source is available.

explanation: Enterprise architecture and workflow interoperability is the capability to design statistical systems and workflows so they work together across programs using shared standards, modular components, metadata-driven orchestration, and reusable automation. In practice, this means building production, processing, and workflow configurations that are interoperable, auditable, version-controlled, and scalable from the outset, rather than creating custom or siloed solutions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 2.5, 2.6, and 3.4 requires staff to design and configure systems for modular reuse, automation, metadata-driven workflows, self-service business development, and clear business-IT integration within enterprise guardrails. These requirements are driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize modernized digital operations, interoperability, standardization, agility, and scalable enterprise platforms, thereby expanding system analysis and design expectations beyond traditional technical design and processing.

explanation: Enterprise data ecosystem awareness is the capability to understand and navigate the organization’s full data, systems, registries, catalogues, and service landscape so staff can quickly find, assess, and reuse existing assets before proposing new collection. In future work, this supports needs identification, concept identification, and data availability assessment by requiring staff to use enterprise discovery tools, metadata, and standardized processes to evaluate internal, administrative, and alternative sources in a more systematic and automation-ready way.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more enterprise-wide, digitally enabled, and reuse-first approaches to identifying needs and assessing data options. These change drivers influence future work requirements by making formal scanning of agency holdings, metadata-assisted discovery, automation compatibility, and evidence-based justification for any new survey or bespoke collection essential at the outset of GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5.

explanation: Comparative solution assessment is the capability to formally evaluate current assets, reuse options, automation opportunities, process redesign choices, and new collection proposals against clear criteria such as cost, risk, quality, reusability, and strategic fit. In the future state, this work must be evidence-based, documented, and supported by metadata, dashboards, and automated screening tools so staff can justify decisions quickly and consistently across needs identification, data suitability review, and ongoing evaluation.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive greater reuse of existing data, stronger digital and automation-enabled decision-making, and more transparent, auditable business cases before launching new collection or redesign work. These change drivers directly increase the need for staff to compare options systematically in activities 1.1, 1.5, and 8.2, using automated discovery, continuous benchmarking, and documented evidence to avoid duplication, support rapid intervention, and ensure alignment with future operational requirements.

explanation: Enterprise feasibility and intake analysis is the capability to assess new data needs early and consistently across the organization using standardized methods, digital tools, and governance-ready documentation. It includes scanning existing internal, administrative, and alternative data assets, evaluating AI and automation options, testing digital workflow and sustainability fit, and clearly documenting when new collection is truly required.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively push the organization toward reuse of existing data, greater automation, stronger digital integration, and more transparent enterprise decision-making. These change drivers reshape GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 by requiring broader and earlier intake analysis, automated data and concept discovery, formal justification for new surveys, and synthesized recommendations that support governance, auditability, and sustainable future operations.

skill_gap: Business intelligence and discovery tool usage
explanation: This capability is the ability to use dashboards, metadata catalogues, search tools, and discovery platforms to quickly find and assess existing data, concepts, and system assets that could meet a business need. In future work, it supports earlier and broader feasibility studies by enabling structured scans of internal, administrative, and alternative data sources, documenting when existing assets are insufficient, and informing decisions about automation, sustainability, and whether new collection is truly necessary.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires staff to identify needs, concepts, and data availability through standardized digital discovery, metadata-assisted scanning, and evidence-based triage before proposing new surveys. These change drivers directly influence GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 by making rapid asset discovery, automated suitability screening, and formal justification of gaps essential to future work requirements.

skill_gap: Enterprise digital architecture and interoperability standards
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess whether proposed processing, analysis, and dissemination solutions fit enterprise digital architecture expectations, including interoperability, reuse, automation, interface standards, and alignment with approved platforms. In practice, it supports designing and selecting modular, metadata-driven, version-controlled components and services that can operate across programs, integrate into automated pipelines, and avoid unnecessary custom or manual builds.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to standardized enterprise platforms, reusable modular services, automation, AI-enabled workflows, and open interoperable dissemination by default. Across GSBPM 2.5, 3.2, and 3.3, these change drivers shift expectations from subject-matter-focused change assessment to judging whether solutions meet enterprise standards for interoperability, auditability, reuse, and governed deployment, making enterprise digital architecture knowledge essential to future work requirements.

skill_gap: Agency data holdings and reuse opportunities
explanation: This capability is the ability to identify and assess existing agency data holdings, administrative and alternative sources, shared platforms, and reusable services before proposing new collection or custom development. It supports a future-state workflow where needs identification, data availability assessment, and collection design are driven by interoperability, automation, metadata, and reuse, so new surveys or bespoke builds are pursued only when clearly justified.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires staff to test reuse, automation, and digital alignment at the start of work, not after a solution has already been chosen. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 3.1, these change drivers shift expectations toward enterprise-wide data discovery, automated suitability screening, and modular reusable platforms, which means officers must be able to challenge manual or custom approaches and justify any exception with evidence.

skill_gap: Option analysis using cost-efficiency and resource-justification frameworks
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess solution options—manual, custom, reused, or automated—using structured cost-efficiency and resource-justification frameworks to determine the most sustainable and operationally viable approach. In future GSBPM activities such as identifying needs, checking data availability and suitability, and designing processing and analysis, staff must prioritize interoperable, reusable, and automation-compatible options, and only support bespoke or manual approaches when a clear evidence-based exception is documented.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires staff to make early, evidence-based decisions that favour reuse, digital alignment, automation, and enterprise sustainability over default manual or custom solutions. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5, these change drivers shift expectations toward standardized, metadata-driven, and resource-conscious workflows, meaning officers must be able to explicitly challenge non-reusable approaches and justify any exception against cost, operational constraints, and long-term maintainability.

explanation: Digital-by-design systems thinking is the capability to design processing and production workflows as modular, reusable, interoperable, and automated components that fit enterprise platforms rather than isolated program-specific solutions. In practice, it means building version-controlled, metadata-driven, auditable pipelines that support standardization, rapid reuse, self-service configuration, and scalable integration across programs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 2.5, 2.6, and 3.2 requires staff to move beyond functional system delivery toward enterprise design for interoperability, automation, reuse, and governance by default. This direction is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-by-default service delivery, standard platforms, responsible automation, and organization-wide scalability, thereby increasing the need for modular, metadata-driven, and cross-program workflow design capabilities.

skill_gap: Automation frameworks and workflow orchestration concepts
explanation: This capability is the knowledge needed to design and configure production systems as modular, automated, and reusable workflows rather than one-off solutions. It includes understanding pipeline design, workflow orchestration, version control, auditability, metadata-driven processing, and the use of standardized components or self-service tools so systems can scale, integrate, and adapt with minimal manual intervention.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 2.6, 3.4, and 3.2 requires staff to build and configure interoperable, version-controlled, and auditable workflows using shared components, orchestration platforms, and automation-first design principles. This direction is driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-by-default service delivery, enterprise reuse, standardization, and modernized production systems—thereby making automation frameworks and workflow orchestration essential to meeting future operational requirements.

skill_gap: Requirements engineering for interoperability and compliance
explanation: This capability is the ability to convert digital standards, interoperability rules, and automation requirements into clear system, database, and test specifications that can be implemented consistently across platforms. It ensures specifications support standardized interfaces, reusable components, automated integration testing, auditability, and compliance by design across processing, data integration, and production system testing activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires statistical production systems to be modular, interoperable, automation-ready, and governed through standardized digital guardrails, while current specification practices remain focused mainly on testing and maintenance. It is also reinforced by Mandate letters emphasizing modern, secure, and integrated digital government, which means future requirements for GSBPM 2.5, 3.5, and 5.1 now include formal proof of compliance, reusable design, automated approvals, and integration readiness that current capability does not fully support.

explanation: This capability is the ability to define and document the compliance evidence, approval checkpoints, and assurance criteria needed for digital-ready statistical systems. It includes specifying how solutions demonstrate interoperability, reuse, automation readiness, auditability, and exception handling so that processing, testing, and deployment can move through standardized and increasingly automated approval flows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires specification work to produce structured proof of digital compliance, FAIR alignment, interoperability, and automation readiness—not just technical requirements. Across GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 3.5, the shift to metadata-driven design, reusable components, automated testing, and attestation-based sign-off means staff must be able to define compliance checkpoints and documentation expectations that align with organizational guardrails and mandate-driven digital priorities.
